interview_metadata.name: Jailyn Claybon
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) — Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I was born and raised in Jacksonville, Florida, mostly around the Southside and with a lot of family roots in older Black neighborhoods like LaVilla and the Northside. My childhood was church, cookouts, school, cousins running in and out, and my mama making sure we knew how to speak to elders and help out before we sat down. I grew up singing in church choir, going to Juneteenth events, and spending weekends with family where somebody was always frying fish or making greens. I was never the most organized kid, but I was steady when things got tense, and people would always say I had a calm way about me. In high school I got into volleyball and dance, especially hip-hop and Zumba-style classes, and I started thinking about health care after helping my grandma when she had blood pressure problems. After I graduated, I started community college and began working toward nursing, but I did not go straight through perfectly. Money, work hours, and just being young made it kind of stop-and-go. I became a nursing assistant, and that really changed how I saw myself because I learned I could handle real responsibility: checking vitals, helping patients bathe, documenting in the EHR, doing basic wound care, and staying calm when a patient or family member was scared. Right now I am 21, never married, no kids, working as a nursing assistant, taking prerequisites toward my ADN, and trying to become an RN focused on community health in Black neighborhoods here in Jacksonville. My life is not fancy, but it feels like it has direction.

follow_ups.question: Who were the main people around you when you were growing up?
follow_ups.response: My mama, my dad, my younger brother, my grandma on my mama's side, and a bunch of cousins. My grandma was the one who kept everybody connected.

follow_ups.question: What did a normal weekend look like for you as a teenager?
follow_ups.response: Saturday might be volleyball, helping clean, or going to Riverside Arts Market with friends, and Sunday was church, choir, food, and then Jaguars football if it was season.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: The biggest crossroads was after high school when I was trying to decide whether to just work full time or actually stay with nursing school. I had friends going different ways, some working retail or service jobs, some leaving Jacksonville, and I was tired of being broke and waiting on school. Around that time my grandma had a scare with her blood pressure, and I was the one writing down her readings and asking questions at appointments. A CNA program felt like a faster way to get in the field, so I did that while taking classes part time. It made me realize I did not just like the idea of nursing; I liked the actual work of caring for people. That choice gave me a real path toward becoming an RN.

follow_ups.question: Was there a specific day or conversation that pushed you toward the CNA route?
follow_ups.response: My auntie told me, 'If you already helping everybody, get paid and get trained for it.' That stuck with me.

follow_ups.question: What would the other path have looked like?
follow_ups.response: Probably working full time at a store or restaurant and saying I would go back to school later, but maybe not actually doing it.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It was both. The pressure kind of happened around me, but signing up for the CNA program was a conscious choice. I remember deciding I needed something that moved me forward, not just something that paid for the week.

follow_ups.question: Did you talk it over with anyone first?
follow_ups.response: Yes, mostly my mama, my auntie, and one older nurse from church.

follow_ups.question: How did you know it was the right choice?
follow_ups.response: Once I started clinicals, I felt nervous but useful, and that felt different from other jobs.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: Yes. More guidance about financial aid, nursing prerequisites, and scheduling would have helped. I had to figure out a lot by asking around, and it would have been easier if the school or a mentoring program had walked me through it.

follow_ups.question: What kind of help would have mattered most?
follow_ups.response: A clear plan showing what classes to take, what deadlines mattered, and how to balance work hours.

follow_ups.question: Did any organization help at all?
follow_ups.response: The Jacksonville Urban League events and people at church gave encouragement, but not a full step-by-step plan.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I am not married, I do not have children, and I am not living with a partner. My mama is probably my closest family person; she checks on me even when I act like I have it handled. My younger brother is still finding his way, and I try to be a good example without bossing him too much. My grandma is important because she is the family storyteller and the reason I care so much about blood pressure screenings and health education. I have aunties, cousins, and church family who feel like family too. We do Sunday dinners sometimes, birthdays, choir events, and family group chats that are always busy. I lean on them emotionally, but I also like having some independence now.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see your mother or grandmother?
follow_ups.response: I see my mama at least once a week and my grandma usually every other week, sometimes more if she needs help.

follow_ups.question: Are you dating anyone right now?
follow_ups.response: Not seriously. I have talked to people, but school and work are taking most of my focus.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: My dad is in my life too. We are not as emotionally close as me and my mama, but he shows up, helps with car stuff, and asks about school.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk with him often?
follow_ups.response: Maybe once or twice a week, usually quick calls or texts.

follow_ups.question: Does he live nearby?
follow_ups.response: Yes, he is still in Jacksonville.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: My friends are a big part of my life. My closest friend is Taniya, who does Zumba with me and will come over while I cook. I have volleyball friends from the Jacksonville Suns club, and we practice or play on the beach when schedules line up. I am also close with a few coworkers from the nursing facility because when you work hard shifts together, you learn who is solid. Church choir people are important too, especially the older women who check on me like aunties.

follow_ups.question: Who do you spend the most casual time with?
follow_ups.response: Taniya and my volleyball friend Bri. We might grab smoothies, go dance, or watch a game.

follow_ups.question: How often are you with friends in person?
follow_ups.response: Usually two or three times a week, depending on work and class.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: I live in the 32246 area of Jacksonville, more on the Southside. It is convenient because I can get to work, school, the beach, grocery stores, and church without everything being too far. There are apartments, shopping centers, busy roads, and a mix of families, students, and working people. It is not the same neighborhood feeling as where some of my older family grew up, but it is practical. I like that I can get to Riverside for the arts market or out toward the Timucuan Preserve when I want a nature break.

follow_ups.question: What places do you go to most near home?
follow_ups.response: Publix or Walmart, the gym for Zumba, a coffee place to study, and sometimes the beach if I have time.

follow_ups.question: Do you know your neighbors?
follow_ups.response: A little. I know faces and say hey, but it is not super close.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel mostly safe, especially during the day. At night I pay attention, park near lights, and do not linger outside alone because car break-ins and weird stuff can happen anywhere.

follow_ups.question: Have you personally had anything happen there?
follow_ups.response: Nothing major, just one time someone went through cars in the lot.

follow_ups.question: What do you do to feel safer?
follow_ups.response: I lock everything, carry my phone, and text my roommate when I am coming in late.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The upside is convenience and being close to things I need. The downside is rent is high, traffic on the main roads gets annoying, and sometimes it feels a little disconnected compared with a neighborhood where everybody knows each other.

follow_ups.question: What do you like least day to day?
follow_ups.response: Traffic and the cost of rent.

follow_ups.question: Would you stay in this area long term?
follow_ups.response: Maybe for school and work, but later I want somewhere with more community feel.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: I share a two-bedroom apartment with my friend and roommate Taniya. She works front desk at a dental office and is also taking classes. We are both busy, so the apartment can get a little lived-in, but we try to keep the kitchen and bathroom decent. We split rent and utilities, and sometimes we cook together or watch shows after work.

follow_ups.question: How long have you lived together?
follow_ups.response: About nine months.

follow_ups.question: How do you divide chores?
follow_ups.response: We try to alternate trash, dishes, and cleaning, but honestly we remind each other a lot.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Everyone is permanent. It is just me and Taniya on the lease.

follow_ups.question: Is anyone staying for more than a few nights?
follow_ups.response: No, not right now.

follow_ups.question: Do you expect that to change soon?
follow_ups.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: Sometimes my cousin or one of Taniya's sisters may sleep over after a late night, but not often.

follow_ups.question: How often does that happen?
follow_ups.response: Maybe once a month.

follow_ups.question: Is it usually planned?
follow_ups.response: Mostly spontaneous.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, nobody usually lives here who is away.

follow_ups.question: No one away at school?
follow_ups.response: No.

follow_ups.question: No one hospitalized or traveling long term?
follow_ups.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: My week changes based on my work schedule. On workdays I am usually up around 5:30 or 6:00, get coffee, pack food if I remembered, and head to the facility for a day shift. On class days I might work a shorter shift or study at night. Mondays and Wednesdays are often school or study days, and a couple evenings I do Zumba or volleyball. Sundays are slower if I am off: church, choir, family food, and Jaguars if it is football season. My schedule is not always neat, which is something I am trying to improve.

follow_ups.question: What time do you usually go to bed?
follow_ups.response: Around 11:30, but later if I am charting notes for school or scrolling.

follow_ups.question: What is the first thing you do most mornings?
follow_ups.response: Check my phone, then coffee or water, then scrubs if I work.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I work as a nursing assistant at a skilled nursing and rehab facility. My main duties are helping patients with activities of daily living, taking vital signs, reporting changes, helping with transfers, doing basic wound care support, and documenting in the EHR. I usually work three or four shifts a week, often 7 a.m. to 3 p.m., with some weekends. Sometimes I pick up an extra shift if money is tight. The work is physical and emotional, but I like feeling useful.

follow_ups.question: Which tasks take the most time?
follow_ups.response: Morning care, vitals, call lights, and documenting everything before the shift ends.

follow_ups.question: Do you work nights?
follow_ups.response: Not usually. I have covered evening shifts before, but days fit school better.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I help my grandma with health stuff sometimes, like checking her blood pressure or helping her understand instructions after appointments. I also volunteer at community health fairs when I can, mostly doing basic education and helping people find screening tables. I sing in church choir, so rehearsal is usually one evening a week. Then there is regular adult stuff like laundry, groceries, bills, and trying to keep up with assignments.

follow_ups.question: How often do you volunteer?
follow_ups.response: Maybe once every month or two, more if a church health event comes up.

follow_ups.question: What responsibility is easiest to fall behind on?
follow_ups.response: Laundry and keeping my planner updated.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: Recently I started being more serious about my ADN prerequisites, so I blocked off study time instead of just fitting it in whenever. I also added a Zumba class back into my week because I was feeling stiff and stressed from work. My facility has been short-staffed at times, so some weeks I get asked to pick up shifts. That can throw off school and sleep if I am not careful.

follow_ups.question: What changed your mind about studying more intentionally?
follow_ups.response: I missed a quiz deadline once, and that embarrassed me enough to get stricter.

follow_ups.question: What helps you stick to the new routine?
follow_ups.response: Phone reminders, Taniya asking if I studied, and going to coffee shops where I focus better.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: I do not have children, so I do not have a school-year routine for kids. I do help with younger cousins sometimes, but not as a daily responsibility.

follow_ups.question: Do you babysit often?
follow_ups.response: Maybe once in a while for family, not weekly.

follow_ups.question: Do you want children someday?
follow_ups.response: Maybe someday, but not until I am more settled in my career.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: Personally I have not had a major law enforcement experience beyond traffic stops or seeing police around. But being a young Black woman, I think about it. My family taught me early to stay calm, keep my hands visible, and not argue on the side of the road. That is sad that it has to be a lesson, but it is real. I have also seen police presence feel different depending on the neighborhood.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever been pulled over?
follow_ups.response: Once for a brake light. It was fine, but I was nervous the whole time.

follow_ups.question: What did you do during that stop?
follow_ups.response: I kept my hands on the wheel, answered politely, and called my mama afterward.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: During protests and community events after George Floyd, seeing police lined up downtown stayed with me. It made me feel both protected and watched, if that makes sense.

follow_ups.question: Were you at those events?
follow_ups.response: I went to one local march with friends and church people.

follow_ups.question: Was it peaceful?
follow_ups.response: The part I attended was peaceful, mostly chanting and people speaking.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have never been arrested. I have a cousin who got arrested for a nonviolent charge when I was in high school, and that affected the family because court costs and transportation were stressful.

follow_ups.question: Are they doing okay now?
follow_ups.response: Yes, they are working now and trying to keep things steady.

follow_ups.question: Did that change how you think about the system?
follow_ups.response: Yes, it showed me how one mistake can turn into a lot of fees and barriers.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote in presidential elections and I am trying to be better about local elections. At 18 I was excited to register, but honestly local races used to confuse me. Now I pay more attention because health care, rent, transportation, policing, and school funding are all local too. I would not say I am perfect, but I do care.

follow_ups.question: Did you vote in the most recent major election?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I voted.

follow_ups.question: How do you decide who to vote for?
follow_ups.response: I look at health care, education, wages, racial justice, and whether they seem connected to regular people.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I would say I lean Democratic, especially on health care, education, racial justice, and workers being treated fairly. I am not the type to argue politics all day online, but my values are pretty clear. I believe people should have access to preventive care before they end up in the ER. I think Black neighborhoods in Jacksonville deserve investment, safe housing, good schools, and clinics that treat people with respect. I also care about reproductive health and people being able to make decisions with their doctors. I get frustrated with both parties sometimes because politicians talk big and then regular people are still struggling. But when I look at the issues that matter to me, I am definitely closer to Democrats.

follow_ups.question: What issue feels most personal to you?
follow_ups.response: Health care access, especially blood pressure, diabetes, and preventive screenings in Black communities.

follow_ups.question: Do your friends mostly agree with you?
follow_ups.response: Most of my close friends lean similar, though some are less political and just tired of everybody.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I have become more local-minded. Before, politics felt like presidents and big arguments. Working in health care and seeing patients deal with insurance, transportation, and family caregiving made me realize policy shows up in small daily ways. I also became more serious about housing costs because rent has been hitting people my age hard. I am less impressed by slogans now and more interested in what actually gets funded.

follow_ups.question: Was there a specific moment that changed you?
follow_ups.response: Seeing a patient delay follow-up care because of cost really stuck with me.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk about these changes with family?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially with my mama and aunties after church or during Sunday dinner.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: They affected me a lot. It was not like racism was new to me, but seeing the videos and then seeing people debate whether what happened was wrong was heavy. It made me think about my brother, my cousins, my patients, and how Black people have to calculate safety in ways other people may not notice. It also pushed me toward wanting community health work because racism affects stress, trust, and health.

follow_ups.question: How did it affect you emotionally?
follow_ups.response: I felt angry, sad, and tired, especially when people acted like asking for accountability was too much.

follow_ups.question: Did it affect your relationships?
follow_ups.response: It made me notice who was willing to listen and who wanted to dismiss it.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think the issues are about more than one police encounter. It is about whose pain gets believed, whose neighborhoods get resources, and who gets treated as a threat first. I do think communities need safety, and I respect good public servants, but accountability has to be real. I also think health care is connected because stress from racism shows up in bodies over time.

follow_ups.question: What does accountability mean to you?
follow_ups.response: Clear consequences for misconduct, better training, transparency, and not protecting people just because they have a badge.

follow_ups.question: Do you see this as connected to your career?
follow_ups.response: Yes, because trust and health education go together in communities that have been mistreated.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think a lot about how race is both history and everyday life. In Jacksonville, you can see Black excellence, Black churches, businesses, artists, and families holding each other up. But you can also see gaps in health, schools, wages, and policing. I try not to let it make me bitter, but I also do not want to pretend everything is equal. I want to be part of solutions that are practical and rooted in community.

follow_ups.question: Where do you see Black excellence locally?
follow_ups.response: At church, Juneteenth events, Riverside artists, nurses I look up to, and groups like the Jacksonville Urban League.

follow_ups.question: What feels most unfair to you?
follow_ups.response: That people can work hard and still not have the same access to care, safety, or opportunity.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I have talked with family and friends, shared some posts, and went to one peaceful march in Jacksonville. I am not out protesting every week, but I try to stay informed and show up when I can.

follow_ups.question: Who did you attend the march with?
follow_ups.response: Taniya, one cousin, and some church members.

follow_ups.question: Do you post about it online?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes on Instagram stories, but I try not to get pulled into comment fights.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: My family talks about it openly, especially the older people who connect it to what they saw growing up. My younger friends are more likely to post, share resources, or go to events. Some coworkers avoid the topic at work because patients and staff have different views. In my close circle, most people care about the issue, but they show it differently.

follow_ups.question: Does anyone close to you disagree strongly?
follow_ups.response: Not strongly close to me, but I know people who think talking about race makes things worse.

follow_ups.question: How do you handle that?
follow_ups.response: I try to stay calm and ask what they mean, but I will step away if it gets disrespectful.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: Overall I am healthy. I stay active through volleyball, Zumba, and being on my feet at work. I do get tired and sometimes my back or feet hurt after long shifts, but nothing diagnosed as chronic. I try to eat balanced, though I love soul food and fried catfish, so I play with healthier versions like collard-green quinoa bowls. My biggest health issue is probably sleep consistency and stress.

follow_ups.question: Do you have any diagnosed medical conditions?
follow_ups.response: No diagnosed chronic conditions.

follow_ups.question: Do you have a primary care doctor?
follow_ups.response: Yes, though I am not as consistent with checkups as I should be.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: It is easy when I am dancing, playing volleyball, or cooking at home because those feel natural to me. It is hard when work is short-staffed and I come home exhausted, because then I grab fast food or skip exercise. Money matters too because healthier groceries and gym stuff add up. My schedule being loose can make it harder.

follow_ups.question: What healthy habit are you best at keeping?
follow_ups.response: Moving my body, especially dance or volleyball.

follow_ups.question: What habit is hardest?
follow_ups.response: Sleeping on time and meal prepping.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: Nothing major like a diagnosis or broken bone. I did strain my ankle playing beach volleyball last year, and I had to rest it for a couple weeks. I also had one period where I felt really run down from work and school, like headaches and bad sleep. That made me pay more attention to hydration and not taking every extra shift.

follow_ups.question: Did you see a doctor for the ankle?
follow_ups.response: I went to urgent care to make sure it was not broken.

follow_ups.question: Did it affect work?
follow_ups.response: A little. I had to move slower and wear a brace.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: My health has not stopped me from working long term. When my ankle was strained, I had to be careful, and when I am exhausted, I am less patient, but I still manage.

follow_ups.question: Have you missed work for health reasons recently?
follow_ups.response: Only a sick day here and there.

follow_ups.question: Do you worry about injury at work?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially lifting or transfers if we are short-staffed.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: Yes, my grandma's blood pressure has been the main thing. She is doing okay, but she needs reminders and support with appointments and understanding what the doctor said. In my family, diabetes and high blood pressure are things we talk about. That is part of why I care about community health and screenings so much.

follow_ups.question: What do you do to help your grandmother?
follow_ups.response: I check readings, remind her about medication, and go over discharge papers or appointment notes.

follow_ups.question: Does anyone else help?
follow_ups.response: My mama and aunties help too.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: I have not gone without emergency care, but I have delayed routine things because of cost, scheduling, or not wanting to miss work. My family has had those moments too, where you wait and see because a copay or transportation is inconvenient. Working in health care makes me more aware of how hard the system is to navigate. Even people with insurance can feel lost.

follow_ups.question: What care have you delayed?
follow_ups.response: Dental cleaning once and a regular checkup.

follow_ups.question: What makes access easier?
follow_ups.response: Flexible clinic hours, clear insurance information, and having someone explain next steps.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: My family uses home remedies in a Southern way, like ginger tea, honey, lemon, steam, Epsom salt baths, and prayer. My grandma has certain teas she trusts. I do not use that instead of medical care if something is serious, but I do see comfort in it. Church prayer is part of how my family handles illness too.

follow_ups.question: What was the most recent home remedy you used?
follow_ups.response: Honey and lemon tea when my throat was scratchy.

follow_ups.question: Do you tell doctors about those remedies?
follow_ups.response: If it matters, yes, especially if it is something taken regularly.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: I do not smoke. I drink socially sometimes, like a margarita or wine when I am out with friends, but not as a main coping tool. When I am stressed I am more likely to dance, cook, sing, or call somebody. I have seen enough health issues to be careful with using alcohol to handle emotions.

follow_ups.question: How often do you drink?
follow_ups.response: Maybe a couple times a month, usually one or two drinks.

follow_ups.question: What do you do after a bad shift?
follow_ups.response: Shower, eat, vent to Taniya, and maybe put on J. Cole or Anderson .Paak.

transcript.question_text: Other people say they cope by relying on prescriptions, pain medications, marijuana, or other substances. How about for you and can you describe your most recent experience of using them, if any?
transcript.response: I do not use marijuana or other substances. I take over-the-counter ibuprofen or acetaminophen if my feet or back hurt after work, but I try not to overdo it. The most recent time was after a long shift when my back was sore from helping with transfers. I took ibuprofen, stretched, and used a heating pad.

follow_ups.question: Do you have any prescriptions you rely on?
follow_ups.response: No regular prescriptions.

follow_ups.question: Do friends around you use marijuana?
follow_ups.response: Some do socially, but it is not really my thing.

transcript.question_text: How are you and your family coping with, or paying for, your health care needs right now?
transcript.response: I have basic health coverage through work, though it is not amazing. I budget for copays when I know something is coming. My family uses insurance where they have it, clinics when needed, and we help each other with rides or small costs. A lot of coping is planning, asking questions, and trying not to let small health stuff become big.

follow_ups.question: Are medical bills a major debt for you?
follow_ups.response: No, not right now.

follow_ups.question: Who helps older relatives get to appointments?
follow_ups.response: My mama, aunties, and sometimes me.

transcript.question_text: Some people are excited about medical vaccination, and others, not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: I am generally pro-vaccine, especially working in health care. I understand why some people are cautious, especially in Black communities with medical mistrust, but I believe good information and respectful conversations matter.

follow_ups.question: Do you get flu shots?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially because of work.

follow_ups.question: How do you talk to hesitant relatives?
follow_ups.response: I try not to shame them. I ask what they are worried about and share what I know.

transcript.question_text: What are your trusted sources of information about the vaccine?

transcript.question_text: Now we're going to talk a bit more about what life was like for you over the past year. Tell me all about how you have been feeling.
transcript.response: This past year has been a mix of proud, tired, hopeful, and sometimes overwhelmed. I feel proud because I am working, paying bills, and moving toward nursing. Dance, choir, cooking, and talking to my close friends help me come back to myself.

follow_ups.question: What emotion has been strongest lately?
follow_ups.response: Pressure, but not hopeless pressure. More like I know I am building something.

follow_ups.response: Taniya and my mama notice first.

transcript.question_text: Tell me a story about a time in the last year when you were in a rough place or struggling emotionally.
transcript.response: A few months ago I missed a school deadline after picking up extra work shifts. I felt embarrassed and like maybe I was not disciplined enough for nursing school. I cried in my car after work because I was tired and mad at myself. Then I called my mama, and she talked me down but also told me to make a real plan. That is when I started using phone reminders and blocking study time.

follow_ups.question: Did the instructor let you make up the work?
follow_ups.response: Partly, but I lost some points.

follow_ups.question: What did that teach you?
follow_ups.response: That relaxed scheduling can cost me, even if my intentions are good.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they struggle with depression, anxiety, or something else like that. How about for you?

Sometimes after hard patient situations I feel heavy. I usually cope by talking it out, praying, dancing, or taking a quiet drive.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever gone to counseling?
follow_ups.response: No, but I am open to it if I felt stuck.

follow_ups.question: What signs tell you stress is building?
follow_ups.response: I get quiet, my room gets messy, and I start procrastinating.

follow_ups.response: My mama, because she worries about everybody.

follow_ups.question: How does the family support each other?
follow_ups.response: Food, rides, prayer, cash app when someone is short, and checking in.

It is not just Sunday service; it is aunties checking on you, health fairs, youth events, food drives, and a place where people know your family. follow_ups.question: How often do you attend church?

transcript.question_text: What is or was your occupation? In this occupation, what kind of work do you do and what are the most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: I am a nursing assistant at a skilled nursing and rehabilitation facility. My work is hands-on patient care: helping residents bathe, dress, eat, transfer, and move safely. I take vital signs, report changes to nurses, help with basic wound care support, follow infection control protocols, and document care in the electronic health record. The most important duties are noticing changes, keeping patients clean and safe, protecting dignity, and communicating clearly with nurses and families. It can be heavy work, but I like being part of somebody's healing or comfort.

follow_ups.response: Yes.

follow_ups.question: Did you ever visit her workplace?
follow_ups.response: A few times when I was younger.

transcript.question_text: Did your dad work for pay for at least a year while you were growing up?
transcript.response: Yes, my dad worked for pay.

follow_ups.question: Was he consistently employed?
follow_ups.response: Mostly, yes.

follow_ups.question: Did he work full time?
follow_ups.response: Yes, most of the time.

transcript.question_text: What was his job? What kind of work did he do? What were his most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: My dad worked as an auto mechanic and later did maintenance work. He fixed cars, diagnosed problems, changed parts, handled oil changes, brakes, and electrical issues. He is good with his hands and practical problem-solving.

follow_ups.question: Did he teach you anything about cars?
follow_ups.response: Basic stuff, like checking oil, tires, and not ignoring warning lights.

follow_ups.question: Did his work affect family life?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes he worked long hours, but he could help family with car problems.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did he work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where he worked?
transcript.response: He worked at auto repair shops and later for a maintenance service company. The repair shops fixed customers' vehicles, and the maintenance company handled repairs for buildings and equipment. It was hands-on service work.

follow_ups.question: Was it locally owned?
follow_ups.response: Some places were local shops.

follow_ups.question: Did he own a business?
follow_ups.response: No, but he did help people on the side sometimes.

transcript.question_text: We all have hopes about what our future will look like. Imagine yourself a few years from now. Maybe you want your life to be the same in some ways as it is now. Maybe you want it to be different in some ways. What do you hope for?
transcript.response: A few years from now, I hope I am an RN with my ADN finished and maybe working on my BSN. I want to specialize in community health nursing and be part of screenings, education, and outreach in underserved Black neighborhoods in Jacksonville. I hope I have a better financial cushion, less debt, and maybe my own place. I still want dance, volleyball, church choir, cooking, and road trips in my life because those keep me feeling like myself. Long term, I dream about starting a community health outreach program with free screenings and mentorship for high school students interested in health care.

follow_ups.question: What would success look like on an ordinary day?
follow_ups.response: Working as a nurse, coming home not completely drained, cooking dinner, and having money saved.

follow_ups.question: Where do you want to travel first?
follow_ups.response: New Orleans, for the music, food, and culture.

transcript.question_text: What do you value the most in your life?
transcript.response: I value family, faith, health, community, and dignity. I care about people being treated like they matter, especially when they are sick, older, scared, or overlooked. I value joy too: music, food, dance, laughter, and being with people who make life lighter. I want my life to be useful, not just busy.

follow_ups.question: Which value guides your work most?
follow_ups.response: Dignity. Patients know when you see them as a whole person.

follow_ups.question: Which value guides your friendships?
follow_ups.response: Loyalty and realness.
